transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-03-03
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Evan (Redwood SE), Dr. Ravi Menon (Peregrine), Janelle Cruz (Security), Tom Alvarez (Eng)

[00:00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro: I'm Samira, AE at Redwood, this is Evan, our solutions engineer.
[00:00:10] Ravi: Thanks, Samira. we wanted to focus on data handling for the POC — mainly what Redwood logs, retention, and PII concerns.
[00:00:20] Samira: Absolutely. high level we'll cover default logging, ability to disable logging, redaction options, retention windows, and where prompts are stored. Evan will jump into technical details.
[00:00:35] Evan: hi all. quick note, apologies if I mangle some product names, sometimes the transcript will show Red wood or Redwood Dedicateed, but yes: Redwood Dedicated and Redwood Private are the two modes we typically discuss for enterprise.
[00:00:50] Janelle: to be clear, our legal team requires that patient identifiers (names, MRNs, dates of birth) are not stored in plain text and logs need to be auditable. we also need to know whether prompts are persisted and for how long.
[00:01:05] Evan: totally. so by default for hosted API, we retain request logs for 30 days for troubleshooting and billing, but customers can opt out of any logging for PII-sensitive traffic — we call that "no-retain" or opt-out logging. for Dedicated or Private deployments, logs remain in your environment and retention is under your control.
[00:01:25] Ravi: okay so Dedicated would be preferable. but we still want to understand what gets written to disk even inside Dedicated — e.g., ephemeral caches, KV cache, and model inputs in traces.
[00:01:38] Evan: good question. runtime components: 1) request traces / audit logs, 2) KV cache for serving performance, 3) temporary process memory. On Dedicated/Private, we can configure audit logs to not include full prompt text — instead store hashes or redacted variants. KV cache is in-memory by default but can be configured to not persist to disk; our default behavior keeps caches in RAM and they are not part of persistent logs.
[00:02:00] Tom: when you say hashes, is that reversible? our security team will ask if hashing could be used to reconstruct inputs.
[00:02:08] Evan: hashing is one-way — we normally use SHA-256 for deterministic de-duplication. if you need additional privacy we can store salted-hashes under your KMS-managed salt. that's in the Private workflow.
[00:02:20] Janelle: what about structured logging? sometimes the model outputs PHI embedded in a returned string, and we don't want that logged. can Redwood strip PII from outputs automatically?
[00:02:33] Samira: yes we have a couple of approaches: client-side redaction (you sanitize before sending), server-side redaction using regex and ML-based detectors, or policy layer that blocks retention of any outputs that match PII detectors. Evan can speak to accuracy and false positives.
[00:02:48] Evan: our ML redactor is tuned for common PII (names, SSN-like numbers, MRNs, dates). it's not perfect; we recommend a hybrid approach — client-side scrub + server-side redaction as a safety net. for POCs we can enable server-side redaction and sample logs for you to review.
[00:03:05] Ravi: sample logs — how will those be shared? we need to ensure redaction happened before logs leave our VPC.
[00:03:12] Evan: for Private/Dedicated, logs stay inside your VPC. for hosted we can run a redaction stage before any logs are sent to Redwood so only redacted artifacts are transmitted. for the POC we'll recommend Dedicated in your AWS account so you control egress.
[00:03:28] Tom: performance-wise, does redaction add latency that could break our SLOs? our user-facing chat needs p50 < 250ms.
[00:03:36] Evan: good point. regex-based redaction is microsecond-level; ML-based redaction is heavier but can be run asynchronously or as a fast on-path detector depending on your latency budgets. for user-facing low-latency paths we usually do a lightweight detector on-path and deeper async checks for logging/retention. with Dedicated instance sizing we can meet p50=200-250ms for our expected workload.
[00:04:00] Ravi: let's talk workloads — our anticipated production workload for the feature is ~200 reqs/sec peak, average 80 reqs/sec, token sizes average 120 tokens per request with spikes to 800 tokens for some clinical summaries.
[00:04:14] Evan: that's helpful. for a POC we'll size to mimic those patterns. recommended POC hardware: 1 x 8-GPU pool (A100 class or equivalent) with batching configured to prioritize latency for chat paths and throughput for background summarization. we'll provide a runner to simulate bursts and long sequences.
[00:04:33] Tom: do you support quantized models to reduce memory usage?
[00:04:36] Evan: yes, we have quantization profiles in Redwood Optimize; for inference we support INT8/4-bit variants. that impacts latency slightly but greatly reduces memory and cost. for the POC we can test both float32 and quantized variants as part of the benchmark.
[00:04:50] Janelle: retention windows — we have a 90-day legal requirement for some logs but PII must be redacted. what retention options do you offer?
[00:04:59] Samira: you can configure retention per log type: request logs, audit logs, metrics. For Dedicated/Private you control retention, and policies can be enforced via our console or IaC. For hosted we have defaults (30 days) with enterprise tier options to extend to 90/365 or to set immediate purge. We can also provide log sinks that ship to your S3 with lifecycle policies.
[00:05:19] Ravi: prompt storage — are prompts stored alongside model metadata? if we send PHI in prompts, does Redwood persist the prompt text?
[00:05:28] Evan: by default we store prompts for debugging and training signals for 30 days on hosted. However, customers can opt out of prompt retention entirely. In Dedicated/Private the decision is yours. For the POC we'll configure prompts to be redacted or hashed before any persistence. we can also implement prompt-ephemeral mode where prompts are not written to disk at all.
[00:05:45] Tom: curious about how you handle function calls / tools. our agents call internal APIs sometimes with patient ids — are those logged?
[00:05:53] Evan: function call payloads follow the same rules as prompts; by default they're logged for observability but can be redacted. we also support token-level masking for logs so you can keep the intent metadata while stripping identifiers.
[00:06:05] Janelle: is audit logging compliant with SOC2? we need immutable audit trails for access to model logs.
[00:06:11] Samira: Redwood provides an audit log feature that records access events, who accessed what, and timestamps. For Dedicated/Private, audit logs are under your control and can be shipped to your SIEM. Our SOC2 report (I'll send) covers hosted audit logging practices.
[00:06:25] Ravi: benchmarks — what will you measure during the POC and how long?
[00:06:29] Evan: proposed benchmark plan: 1) baseline latency (p50/p95/p99) for chat flows at target concurrency; 2) throughput / tokens per second for summarization flows; 3) tail latency under bursts; 4) memory and GPU utilization; 5) correctness/quality checks using your prompt set. We'll run an initial smoke test, then a 3-5 day steady-state run and a 1-2 day stress window.
[00:06:52] Tom: timeline — how long for setup and runs?
[00:06:55] Samira: setup: 1 week to provision Dedicated instance and configs assuming AWS account access; bench harness and sample data shared ASAP. then benchmark week of 2027-03-15; wrap-up and results the following week. overall 4-week POC end-to-end.
[00:07:10] Janelle: legal will want to see a data flow diagram and the KMS integration view.
[00:07:15] Samira: yes — I'll send the security pack with architecture diagrams. Evan will detail KMS options: bring-your-own-key (BYOK) or Redwood-managed keys.
[00:07:24] Evan: BYOK is supported for Private and Dedicated. Keys are used to encrypt persistent artifacts like stored logs and salted-hash salts. Runtime in-memory encryption is also available for attested environments.
[00:07:35] Ravi: about prompt hashing you mentioned salted-hash — who manages the salt?
[00:07:39] Evan: you manage salt in BYOK mode; Redwood can manage it if you prefer but we recommend customer-managed salts for higher assurance.
[00:07:47] Tom: one more ops question: can we filter logs by route/model so that dev/test logs have longer retention but production logs are purged faster?
[00:07:55] Evan: yes per-route retention is supported; Redwood Console exposes per-model/per-route retention and cost tracking.
[00:08:04] Janelle: sample redaction accuracy — can we run a small audit where you show before/after samples so legal is comfortable?
[00:08:10] Samira: absolutely. we'll provide anonymized before/after samples in the security pack and you can run your own checks during the POC.
[00:08:20] Ravi: outstanding risks? thoughts?
[00:08:23] Evan: main risks are: 1) unseen PII patterns that the redactor misses — mitigated by client-side scrub + server-side ML; 2) long sequences that stress KV cache causing memory pressure — mitigated by quantization and kernel selection; 3) integration friction with your KMS — we'll run a quick integration test.
[00:08:43] Samira: recap of success criteria we discussed: a) no plaintext PII persisted (or verified redaction) b) p50 latency < 250ms for chat flows at nominal load c) throughput to handle 200 reqs/sec bursts with acceptable tail latency d) clear audit log delivery to your SIEM or S3 sink.
[00:09:03] Tom: sounds good to me.
[00:09:06] Janelle: agreed pending legal review.
[00:09:08] Samira: next steps recap: I'll send security pack and SOC2; Evan will send benchmark harness and a proposed script; Tom will provide sample data and PII field list; Janelle will confirm retention/legal constraints. we'll aim to start provisioning early next week.
[00:09:25] Ravi: thanks everyone, appreciate the clarity.
[00:09:28] Samira: thanks all, we'll follow up via email and share the docs. bye.

Action items (verbatim shared):
- Samira: send security pack (SOC2, architecture diagrams, KMS guide)
- Evan: benchmark script and harness + test runner
- Tom: anonymized/sanitized sample dataset and PII field list
- Janelle: legal confirmation of retention constraints

End of transcript.
